When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents

Xinyu Wang Affiliation: School of Civil Engineering, The University of Sydney, Darlington 2008 NSW, Australia Affiliation: Corresponding author: xinyu.wang@sydney.edu.au    Andres Fielbaum Affiliation: School of Civil Engineering, The University of Sydney, Darlington 2008 NSW, Australia
Abstract

The EU Platform Work Directive, which member states must transpose by December 2026, obliges ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker’s behaviour affects them. Plain-language rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to hand the disclosed rules to an AI assistant that decides for them. We ask how the two main families of rebalancing policy perform once their rules are public and drivers act on them in this way: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover the requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent that maximizes its own net income and receives either no rules (N) or the rules at the level of detail the directive requires (L). We test the agents in a small three-zone model with ten drivers, and a more realistic city-network, Manhattan. Two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, are evaluated in this study, and both models show equally good comprehension of the system and rules.

Once the rules are disclosed, the drivers follow the platform more closely and decline far fewer of its rebalancing offers: in Manhattan, the share they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the same behaviour has different effects under the two policies, most of all for the platform: disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for repositioning the drivers used to do for free, while A’s profit is unchanged, so the two policies, which tie on profit when every driver complies, end 6.1% apart. In the small model, disclosure raises driver income under both policies and both LLMs, and the share of passengers served by 10 to 18 percentage points. Against full compliance in Manhattan, the self-interested drivers make A a win-win-win, raising driver income, platform profit and the service rate by about 10–12% each. Furthermore, we test mixed fleets, in which only some drivers use an AI agent and the others comply, to understand who gains as AI agents spread. The game among the drivers is close to zero-sum under R and positive-sum under A: under R, the AI drivers’ gain comes from fares taken from the compliant drivers, while under A it comes from serving passengers who would otherwise go unserved, so the compliant drivers gain too and the win-win-win holds. Once again, the two policies respond differently to the same self-interested drivers, and the policy decides whether their gain is taken from others or created for all.

This study shows that under mandatory disclosure with a market of self-interested drivers, rebalancing policies which perform equally well can show opposite results. It also provides a framework to evaluate the performance of different policies under the new information disclosure requirement for ride-hailing platforms, which paves the way for future research on the design of rebalancing policies under information equity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that uses LLM agents to evaluate the impact of information disclosure on the performance of rebalancing policies in ride-hailing platforms.

Keywords: ride-hailing; vehicle rebalancing; algorithmic transparency; Platform Work Directive; large language model agents; strategic drivers; model predictive control

1 Introduction

Ride-hailing platforms allocate work, set prices and move drivers by algorithm; however, the mechanism behind them has not been fully explained to the workers. Directive (EU) 2024/2831 on platform work changes this. Its Article 9 requires a platform to inform workers of the main parameters of its automated decision-making systems, the relative importance of those parameters, and the way in which a worker’s behaviour affects the decisions; Article 2 places pay and the pricing of tasks within scope (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024; Adams-Prassl et al., 2023; Veale et al., 2023; Rosin and Parviainen, 2025). The obligation arrives in a workforce that already tries to work the rules out for itself. Studies of algorithmic management show Uber drivers inferring matching and control rules they cannot see (Möhlmann et al., 2021), assembling a shared reading of the algorithm from clues and tests (Möhlmann et al., 2023), and asking most often for the rules on pricing, promotions, routing and dispatch (Rao et al., 2025). Thus, the question for a platform operator is no longer whether to disclose, but what happens once it must.

Drivers who understand a rule act on it, and the dispatch rule decides what their reaction does to everyone else. Drivers have logged off together to trigger surge pricing (Schröder et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023; Tripathy et al., 2023), cherry-pick requests when the surge mechanism rewards it (Garg and Nazerzadeh, 2022; Ashkrof et al., 2022), and reposition strategically across a network (Afèche et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). Rebalancing, the platform’s own instrument for moving idle drivers, has been studied from the opposite side. Reactive policies use only the current state, covering the requests that were just lost (Alonso-Mora et al., 2017) or applying backpressure to the current imbalance (Kanoria and Qian, 2024), where anticipatory policies plan moves on a demand forecast (Zhang et al., 2016; Iglesias et al., 2018; Engelhardt et al., 2023). Almost all of this work assumes that drivers comply with the moves they are sent, and the few studies that relax the assumption estimate or adapt to driver behaviour rather than disclose the rule (Chen et al., 2024; Brar et al., 2024). How much drivers will understand the disclosed rule, and how they will act on it, is therefore unknown.

As required by law, the disclosed rule will be plain text, which is a natural input for a large language model (LLM). An LLM agent can take the rule as written, weigh it against the market state it is shown and choose an action, without a specified reward function or retraining as Reinforcement Learning (RL) requires. With the rapid development of LLMs, they are already being used as economic agents in laboratory settings (Horton et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), automated decision-makers in markets (Xu et al., 2026), and delegated decision-makers for people (Anthropic, 2026). It is therefore plausible that, once the platform discloses its rules, human drivers can use an LLM agent to make decisions in their own interest. Thus, to evaluate the behaviour of self-interested drivers under such disclosure, this study does not need to ask the LLM to imitate a human driver, but to act as a proxy that a driver could use, whose only objective is the driver’s own net income.

The paper makes three contributions. First, to the best of our knowledge, it is the first study of how drivers act, through an LLM agent, on disclosed rules described in plain language. Second, it shows that stable and general patterns exist across different LLMs and different policies, which reveal intrinsic properties of the on-demand mobility system. Third, it gives operators guidance for the soon-to-be-compulsory disclosure of policies at a time when LLMs are widely used: operators should reconsider and redesign their policies under information equity, and this study provides a framework to evaluate the performance of different policies under the new information disclosure requirement, from a small laboratory model to a realistic city-scale simulation.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature in five parts, from the law that requires disclosure to LLM agents in markets, and states the research gaps that the contributions address. Section 3 describes the ride-hailing system and the two rebalancing policies (Section 3.1), and the AI driver agents, including how the policies are disclosed to them (Section 3.2). Section 4 sets up the small model, the city model, the comprehension test and the metrics of evaluation (Section 4.1), and then reports the results (Section 4.2): the comprehension test and the small model, in which the two LLMs are compared, then the city under the reactive and the anticipatory policy, a comparison of the two policies, and city markets in which only some drivers use an AI agent. Section 5 summarises the findings, draws the consequences for operators and regulators, and points to future work. The appendices give the parameter values, the prompts and disclosed rules, the models and their costs, the comprehension questions, and further results for the small model and the city.

2 Literature Review

This section reviews the literature from five perspectives, each of which studies one necessary part of this study. It starts with the law which forces information disclosure (Section 2.1), then turns to the strategic behaviour of drivers who know the rules (Section 2.2), the literature on rebalancing methods (Section 2.3), the information design literature, which shows that the design of a mechanism affects the results (Section 2.4), and finally the LLM agent literature (Section 2.5). Lastly, Section 2.6 states the research gaps and the contributions of this study that address them.

2.1 Rules must be disclosed: algorithmic management and the Platform Work Directive

Two strands explain why “what happens after disclosure” has only now become a question. The first is legal. Adams-Prassl et al. (2023) set out a blueprint for regulating algorithmic management in which transparency, explanation and human review are the pillars; this is the thinking behind Article 9 of Directive (EU) 2024/2831, which turned the main parameters of automated decisions, their relative importance and the effect of a worker’s behaviour on them into an obligation. Veale et al. (2023) examine how “main parameters” should be read and enforced, and Rosin and Parviainen (2025) compare the directive with the GDPR, the Platform-to-Business Regulation and the AI Act: the directive widens transparency rights beyond all three, but asks for parameters and logic, not formulas. Our disclosure condition L is written to that level. The second strand is organisational and human–computer interaction research on how drivers live with rules they cannot see. Möhlmann et al. (2021) describe Uber drivers under algorithmic matching and control working out rules from their consequences; Möhlmann et al. (2023) theorise this as algorithm sensemaking, a multi-step process of enacting, selecting and retaining interpretations of the algorithm; and Rao et al. (2025), analysing over a million posts in driver forums, find that pricing, promotions, routing and dispatch rules are what drivers most want disclosed. Our condition N is the situation these studies describe, state visible and rules hidden, and L replaces the guessing with the text the law requires.

Both strands judge transparency as a form of worker protection. Neither asks how a self-interested driver would use a disclosed rule, and neither compares dispatch rules once they are disclosed. To evaluate such influence, we put the directive-level text into the experiment as written.

2.2 Driver knows the rule: Strategic behaviour and manipulable pricing

The nearest neighbours of this paper study drivers who understand surge pricing. Yu et al. (2023) show that when prices track online supply, drivers who log off at low prices and return after the surge can form a Nash equilibrium that produces price cycles, and that a price floor removes them. Bai et al. (2023) model providers who hide supply to trigger surge and give, in their Lemma 1, the condition under which collusion does not pay; Tripathy et al. (2023) characterise coordinated log-offs under a known surge rule and the bonus or freeze-period remedies. In each case the known rule is the precondition for the manipulation; we turn that precondition into a treatment. Garg and Nazerzadeh (2022) show that multiplicative surge is not incentive compatible for drivers, who cherry-pick trips, and derive an incentive-compatible driver surge; Ma et al. (2022) give a public spatio-temporal pricing mechanism under which accepting every dispatch is a subgame-perfect equilibrium, the natural reference for a future incentive-compatible anticipatory design. On the empirical side, Ashkrof et al. (2022) estimate from stated-preference data how pickup time, surge income and other attributes govern ride acceptance, and Schröder et al. (2020) document anomalous supply shortages induced by dynamic pricing at 137 locations worldwide.

The theoretical studies take the rule as known and assume that drivers respond to it with perfect rationality, and the empirical ones observe drivers without varying what they are told about the rule. Disclosure is therefore never a variable, and how a driver who is not perfectly rational responds once a rule is disclosed remains unknown.

2.3 Rebalancing: Reactive and Anticipatory

There are two mainstream families of rebalancing methods in ride-hailing, and this study evaluates both of them. Reactive rebalancing, which sends idle vehicles to the requests that were just lost at minimum travel, is the rebalancing step of Alonso-Mora et al. (2017); Kanoria and Qian (2024) show that mirror backpressure, a policy that uses only the current state and no demand rates, is near-optimal in steady state. Anticipatory rebalancing, which optimizes vehicle movements over a horizon on a demand forecast, is the model predictive control (MPC) of Zhang et al. (2016) and its data-driven form in Iglesias et al. (2018). The survey of Zardini et al. (2022) organises autonomous mobility-on-demand (AMoD) control into steady-state flow, MPC and learning-based methods, and our two policy classes follow that taxonomy. Anticipatory repositioning usually wins such comparisons, as in the ride-pooling simulation of Engelhardt et al. (2023), which also serves as the implementation reference for our city model. Anticipation is not limited to the moves of idle vehicles: Wang and Fielbaum (2026a) build it into routing and matching and learn its weight with reinforcement learning, and Wang and Fielbaum (2026b) use short-horizon demand to choose where the last passenger is dropped off.

A smaller literature lets drivers refuse or act strategically. Afèche et al. (2023) analyse a network fluid model with self-interested drivers and show how admission and repositioning control shape the equilibrium; Wang et al. (2025) study strategic relocation in a leader–follower game and identify when relocation subsidies are redundant because drivers already move where the platform wants them, which echoes our finding that accurate repositioning is a win-win. Chen et al. (2024) drop the obedience assumption altogether and estimate acceptance of repositioning recommendations from a field study with 99 drivers; Brar et al. (2024) plan rebalancing under adherence that evolves with the drivers’ experience. The conflict between the operator’s objective and that of individual participants is not limited to drivers: Wang and Fielbaum (2027) show that operator-optimal and user-optimal meeting points in ridepooling diverge systematically, and that the cost of the disagreement concentrates in the zones where the two disagree most and falls more on users than on the operator.

AMoD repositioning assumes vehicles obey. The work on strategic or uncertain compliance treats driver behaviour as something to estimate and adapt to; none of it makes disclosure a variable or compares reactive and anticipatory rules after disclosure. We make declining an offer a driver action, report who pays for it, and claim that the same driver behaviour has opposite effects on others under the two rules.

2.4 Influence of disclosure: strategic-response theory and information design

Theory explains why the answer should depend on the rule rather than on disclosure itself. In strategic classification and mechanism design, the decision rule is told to those it judges. Wang et al. (2023) show that with strategic users, disclosing the algorithm often benefits the firm but not necessarily the users. Ghalme et al. (2021) define the price of opacity when agents must act on a guessed classifier, and Shao et al. (2025) show that hiding the classifier can backfire in the online setting. Gonczarowski et al. (2023) show that the same strategy-proof mechanism, described in different ways, changes how people play. Information design in ride-hailing asks how much the platform should tell drivers about demand: Candogan and Wu (2023) derive the optimal disclosure of the demand state to steer repositioning, and Lian et al. (2026) argue that transparency, control and pay must be judged jointly, the same direction as our finding that the effect of disclosure depends on dispatch.

In this theory the rule is a classifier or a static mechanism with no dynamic, spatial or operational outcome. And none of the studies treats the rule as a text that an agent can read and act on.

2.5 AI agents: LLMs in markets and mechanisms

Horton et al. (2023) propose LLMs as simulated economic agents that can be given endowments, information and preferences. Chen et al. (2023) find that GPT passes revealed-preference rationality tests at a higher level than human subjects. Akata et al. (2025) find that LLMs do well in self-interested repeated games and badly in games that require coordination, a reason to expect individual, uncoordinated self-interest from our agents. Fish et al. (2026) show that GPT-4 pricing agents reach supra-competitive prices when they keep notes across periods; our agents have no memory, so our result is a lower bound on learned collusion. Kleinberg and Raghavan (2021) show that many decision-makers sharing one algorithm make correlated errors, the theory behind the herding risk of a fleet driven by one model. Hoshino et al. (2026) find that LLM agents in strategy-proof matching mechanisms mostly report truthfully and deviate more as the rules become complex. In transport, Liu et al. (2025) propose a framework for modelling transport systems with LLM agents as travellers, and a line of work aligns such agents with observed behaviour: Liu et al. (2026a) align them with mode-choice data through learned traveller personas, Liu et al. (2026b) use a second LLM agent to calibrate traveller agents to day-to-day route choice, and Yan et al. (2026) find human-like sensitivities in the value of travel time of LLMs but differences across models in their magnitude. In platform labour, Xu et al. (2026) survey LLM agents as behavioural simulators and decision-support tools for transportation-enabled service platforms, and Zhang et al. (2026) simulate on-demand delivery with persona-grounded LLM riders. All of these aim at realism rather than at rule exploitation. Outside the academic literature, Anthropic (2026) report an experiment in which people delegated trades to AI agents and stronger models systematically won.

No study has had AI driver agents read the rules a platform actually runs and checked whether they exploit them; the LLM collusion and mechanism studies are abstract markets without spatial, dynamic outcomes; and platform-side LLM dispatch work treats the model as a tool, not as a self-interested driver. Our agents read a rule a platform actually runs and act on it in a dynamic, spatial market.

2.6 Research gaps and contributions

To the best of our knowledge, the literature reviewed above leaves three gaps. Each is stated below together with how this paper addresses it.

  1. 1.

    Disclosure in plain language to self-interested agents. Information equity between the platform and its drivers has not been studied in the form the directive requires: the rule written in plain language and read by a self-interested agent who acts on it. The studies of strategic drivers and strategic response either take the rule as known to rational agents or disclose a classifier, the demand state or a forecast (Sections 2.2 and 2.4), and the LLM-agent studies aim at realism rather than at acting on a disclosed rule (Section 2.5). We address this gap by disclosing the rules in plain language, at the directive’s own level, to LLM driver agents whose only objective is their own net income, and by measuring how the agents act on them.

  2. 2.

    Generality across models, policies and scales. Whether the response to a disclosed rule is a property of the system or of one model and one setting is unknown. LLMs differ from one another in the size of their economic trade-offs (Yan et al., 2026), and the theory of strategic drivers and strategic response is built on stylised models (Sections 2.2 and 2.4). We address this gap by running two unrelated LLMs through the comprehension test and the small model under both policies, where they understand the rules equally well and respond to disclosure in the same direction.

  3. 3.

    Policies under the same disclosure. How different policies perform under the same disclosure has not been studied: rebalancing policies are compared with drivers who comply, and the few studies that relax compliance do not disclose the rule (Section 2.3), so whether a policy that works under compliance still works once its rule is disclosed is unknown. We address this gap by comparing reactive and anticipatory rebalancing under the same disclosure, which gives operators a framework, from a small laboratory model to a city-scale simulation, to evaluate and redesign their policies before disclosure becomes compulsory.

3 Methodology

This section describes the model in two parts. Section 3.1 sets out the ride-hailing system (Section 3.1.1) and the two rebalancing policies compared, reactive (R) and anticipatory (A) (Section 3.1.2). Section 3.2 describes the drivers as AI agents: what they observe (Section 3.2.1), how the platform’s rules are disclosed to them (Section 3.2.2), which decisions they take (Section 3.2.3), and the two language models that take them (Section 3.2.4). The two policies differ in one module of the platform and in one paragraph of the disclosed rules; fares, commission, compensation and every other part of the prompt are shared, so a difference between R and A can only come from dispatch. The two simulation setups on which the method is run, their parameters and the benchmarks are given in Section 4.1. Table 1 summarises the notation.

3.1 Ride-hailing and rebalancing

In ride-hailing, a platform matches passenger requests to drivers, sets the fare of each trip and keeps a commission; the drivers are independent, keep the rest of the fare and pay the cost of driving. Requests and drivers are rarely in the same places at the same time. In the morning, for example, requests start in residential zones while drivers who have just dropped passengers off collect in the business district, and in the evening the flow is reversed. Rebalancing is the platform’s tool for this imbalance: it moves idle drivers from zones with more drivers than requests to zones where requests are going unserved. Here it does so by sending rebalancing offers, which pay a driver a compensation for driving to another zone. Section 3.1.1 describes the system the two policies share, and Section 3.1.2 the two ways of deciding where the offers go.

3.1.1 The ride-hailing system

Zones and time.

The service area is divided into zones, indexed oo, dd or zz (origin, destination, any zone). A trip or move from zone oo to zone dd takes the travel time to​dt_{od} between the zone centres, with to​o=0t_{oo}=0. Time advances in decision steps tt of length Δ​T\Delta T, and the platform works on three clocks: at every decision step it matches waiting requests to idle drivers; at every price interval, of length Δ​Tp\Delta T_{p}, it updates each zone’s fare and the compensation of offers into it; and at every planning interval, of length Δ​Tr\Delta T_{r}, it runs the rebalancing policy and sends rebalancing offers.

Requests and matching.

A passenger requests a trip rr from an origin zone oro_{r} to a destination zone drd_{r} without rejecting any service allocated by the platform. The fleet is a set VV of fVf_{V} vehicles vv, and each carries one request at a time. A waiting request is assigned to an idle driver who can reach the passenger within the maximum pick-up waiting time twmaxt_{w}^{\max}, and then the driver can accept or reject it. A rejected request goes to another eligible driver, and the service will be rejected after a fixed number of rejections or when no eligible driver is left.

Fare.

The fare for each trip composes a base rate which is proportional to the trip length, and a surge term that rises with the shortage of drivers in the origin zone.

where qzq_{z} is the number of requests in zone zz over the last price interval Δ​Tp\Delta T_{p}, s¯z\bar{s}_{z} the idle drivers counted in the zone over that interval and szarrs^{\text{arr}}_{z} the drivers committed to arrive before the next update, either finishing a passenger trip there or driving there on an accepted rebalancing offer. The fare is fixed when the request is made and paid when the trip is completed. The platform keeps a commission θ\theta of the fare as income.

Driver cost.

The cost of a driver comes from two sources: the distance it drives and the time it is online, whether carrying a passenger, moving to a zone or moving on its own. The cost is linear in both, with coefficients βℓ\beta_{\ell} and βT\beta_{T}.

Cv=βℓ​ℓv+βT​Tv,C_{v}=\beta_{\ell}\,\ell_{v}+\beta_{T}\,T_{v}, (3)

where ℓv\ell_{v} is the distance driver vv drives for any reason (passenger trip, pickup, rebalancing move or own move) and TvT_{v} its time online. This cost enters the driver’s net income, Eq. (9).

Driver actions.

A driver can accept or reject a passenger request, accept or decline a rebalancing offer, and stay or move to another zone on their own. There is no offline option. A driver moving on their own earns no compensation.

Rebalancing offers and compensation.

The rebalancing policy (Section 3.1.2) decides which driver should at which time move to which zone. Each such move becomes a rebalancing offer to one idle driver at a time; a declined offer goes to another idle driver in the same zone. An offer to driver vv for zone dd pays the compensation

bv​d=b0​ℓv​d+κv​d​gd,b_{vd}=b_{0}\,\ell_{vd}+\kappa_{vd}\,g_{d}, (4)

a base payment b0b_{0} per unit of the distance ℓv​d\ell_{vd} from the driver’s position to the centre of zone dd, plus a surge payment that rises with the shortage gdg_{d} of the destination at rate κv​d\kappa_{vd}. The coefficients are set so that βℓ​ℓv​d<bv​d<(1−θ)​p​ℓv​d\beta_{\ell}\,\ell_{vd}<b_{vd}<(1-\theta)\,p\,\ell_{vd}: an offer always covers the driving cost and never pays more than the driver’s share of a fare over the same distance, so a move is worth making but never worth more than a passenger. Accepting an offer locks its compensation, which is paid on arrival; only the holder of an offer receives it, and there is no daily cap. Fares, commission, costs and the compensation of Eq. (4) are identical under the two policies. What the two policies decide differently is which offers to send: how many drivers to move, from which zone to which, and at what moment, which Section 3.1.2 explains.

3.1.2 Rebalancing

Both policies share the same decision frequency, information about the system, and pricing and offer mechanics, but differ in what the plan responds to and what it optimizes. The reactive (R) method responds to the requests that have just been lost and covers them with the least travel; the anticipatory (A) method responds to the requests it forecasts and maximizes the platform’s expected profit. The two follow the two mainstream families in the literature (Section 2.3).

Reactive rebalancing (R).

Following the rebalancing step of Alonso-Mora et al. (2017), each plan counts the requests lost in each zone since the last plan and sends idle drivers to cover them with the least travel:

With the definitions of two rebalancing policies and the shared ride-hailing system, the next section describes how drivers make decisions to interact with the platform, as well as how the LLM agents are set up to make those decisions.

3.2 Driver decisions by large language models

Other than the compliant driver baseline (Section 4.2), all experiments in this paper have drivers who make their own decisions, which are modeled by large language models (LLMs). The system status and rebalancing policies are prompted as plain language and serve as the sole input to the LLMs, which return a decision. The LLMs are not trained or rewarded to imitate human drivers, and they have no memory beyond the prompt. They are therefore a stand-in for the assistant a driver could hand the app and the disclosed rules to, and their decisions are self-interested: they maximize their own net income. The drivers of the baseline, by contrast, comply with the platform: they accept every passenger request and rebalancing offer, and never move on their own. The ideal benchmark would be a sophisticated model of how human drivers behave, but such a model, validated for drivers who act on disclosed rules, is hard to obtain. We are therefore transparent about this choice and use compliant drivers as the benchmark, which is also the behaviour that rebalancing policies are usually designed and evaluated for (Section 2.3).

Each driver is represented by an individual LLM, or AI agent, as follows. Whenever that driver has a decision to make, the agent receives one prompt containing the currently available options together with the latest information about the system, and returns one selected option as the chosen action of the driver. The four subsections below explain the process of making decisions by AI agent: how the system is represented as a prompt (Section 3.2.1), how the policies are disclosed to the agent (Section 3.2.2), when and what options are available to the agent, and how the agent makes decisions (Section 3.2.3), and lastly how different LLM models make decisions (Section 3.2.4).

3.2.1 System status inputs

Table 2 summarizes the sections of the prompt that an agent receives when making a decision. [ROLE] gives the agent’s role and objective, and [PLATFORM RULES] the disclosed rules. [TIME] and [YOU] describe the time and the driver’s own state. [YOUR OFFER] and [YOUR REQUEST] describe the offer or request the agent is answering, and appear only then. [MARKET] describes the market in the driver’s zone and the whole city, and [DEMAND] the demand in every zone. The questions follow the prompt; the options for driving to another zone give, for each zone, its fare, the compensation of an offer to it, its idle drivers, recent requests and match rate, and the time, distance and cost of getting there. Appendix B gives the prompts in full. The prompt is updated at every decision step, and the agent receives the latest information about the system when making a decision.

3.2.2 Policy disclosure

The policy is written to the level the directive asks for. It follows Article 9(1)(b)(ii)–(iii): it names the main parameters of the platform’s decisions, their relative importance and how the driver’s behaviour affects the decisions, with no formulas or numbers. It is represented as a section of the prompt with six plain-language paragraphs: how the platform works over time; how the platform matches requests; rebalancing offers; how the platform decides the fares and compensation; how the drivers’ actions affect the platform’s decisions; and how the rebalancing works. The last paragraph describes the active rebalancing policy, which in this study is either reactive or anticipatory; all other paragraphs are always identical.

The details of shared prompts are given in Appendix B. With all information in the prompt, the agent can read the rules and understand how the platform works, and how its own actions affect the platform’s decisions. The next section describes how the agent makes decisions based on this information.

3.2.3 Decisions

A driver has three kinds of decision points, which are summarized in Table 3. The first is when the driver is idle, which happens once every idle-decision interval Δ​Ti\Delta T_{i}. The driver can either stay at its current location, or move to a different zone. If the driver chooses to move, driving cost will be incurred and the driver will not be paid for the movement. During the movement, the driver will still be idle and available to serve any incoming requests. The second is when a passenger request is assigned to the driver. The driver can either accept or reject the request. If the driver accepts the request, it will be committed to serve the passenger until the trip is completed. If the driver rejects the request, it can then choose either to stay at its current location or move to a different zone, which is the same as the idle decision. After rejecting a request, the driver will not be assigned any new requests until the next decision point with duration Δ​T\Delta T. The third is when a rebalancing offer is assigned to the driver. Similar to the request decision, the driver can either accept or reject the offer. If the driver accepts the offer, it will be committed to move to the destination zone and will not be matched with any requests during the trip. If the driver rejects the offer, it can then choose either to stay at its current location or move to a different zone, which is the same as the idle decision. After rejecting an offer, the driver will not be assigned any new offers until the next decision point with duration Δ​Tr\Delta T_{r}.

3.2.4 LLM models

In this study, two LLMs are tested and compared. Considering the cost of running city-scale simulations, the main agent chosen is Jev, a TypeSafe System One model (TypeSafe AI, 2026), which is significantly cost-effective for large-scale simulations. The control agent is Claude Haiku 5.5 with xhigh effort, serving as a reasoning-model benchmark.

Jev.

Jev takes plain-language prompts as input, and returns a set of probabilities over the predefined options, and the option with the highest probability is selected as the decision.

Claude Haiku 5.5.

The reasoning control is Claude Haiku 5.5 at effort xhigh. The same input prompt is sent to the model, and it returns the selected action from the predefined options. The model is designed to have strong reasoning capabilities, and serves as a benchmark for the Jev model.

API calls, costs, version of the models, and other details are given in Appendix D. With the two LLMs set up to make decisions, the next section describes the experiments that put the method to work.

4 Experiments

We evaluate the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes in two experiments. The first is a small three-zone model with ten drivers, which serves as a controlled environment. The second is a city-scale experiment in Manhattan, which shows how the results scale up to a realistic market. We start with the experiment setup, which describes the four test cases.

4.1 Experimental setup

Both experiments cross the two rebalancing policies of Section 3.1.2, reactive (R) and anticipatory (A), with two disclosure conditions, no disclosure (N) and law-level disclosure (L), giving the four test cases of Table 4.

Disclosure conditions.

The condition decides only what the [PLATFORM RULES] section of the prompt (Table 2) contains.

  • •

    No disclosure (N). The [PLATFORM RULES] section is empty, and every other section is identical to L. The agent knows that the platform sets fares, assigns requests and sends rebalancing offers, but not how it makes these decisions, so it can only infer them from the market state and its own history. This is the situation of today’s drivers, who work out from their consequences the rules they cannot see (Möhlmann et al., 2021).

  • •

    Law-level disclosure (L). The [PLATFORM RULES] section holds the six plain-language paragraphs of Section 3.2.2. They are written to the level of Article 9(1)(b)(ii)–(iii) of the directive: the main parameters of the platform’s decisions, their relative importance and how the driver’s behaviour affects them, with no formulas or numbers. The first five paragraphs are the same under R and A; only the rebalancing paragraph (Figure 1) names the active policy.

Under both conditions the agent sees the same past demand, historical demand pattern, market state and own history, as a real driver knows them from experience. Disclosure therefore only provides extra information about the platform’s decision-making process.

Test cases.

R×\timesN and A×\timesN are the platform as drivers know it today, running reactive or anticipatory rebalancing behind rules they cannot see; R×\timesL and A×\timesL are the same platforms once the directive applies. Comparing N with L under one policy measures the effect of disclosure, comparing R with A under one condition measures the effect of the policy, and the difference between the two disclosure effects, the policy ×\times disclosure interaction (Section 4.1.4), shows whether the effect of disclosure depends on the policy. Within an experiment the four cells share everything else, the requests, the start positions and the random seeds, so each comparison changes one factor at a time. The two experiments, a three-zone small model (Section 4.1.1) and Manhattan (Section 4.1.2), are described next; their parameter values are listed in Table 11 (Appendix A).

4.1.1 Small model

To understand the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes, we first test the four cases in a small model with three zones and ten drivers. The small model is a controlled environment to understand how disclosure affects driver behaviour and market outcomes, before the city-scale experiment.

Network and demand.

There are three zones, connected in a line: residential (zone 0), middle (zone 1) and the central business district (zone 2). Travelling between neighbouring zones takes one period, and between the two end zones two periods, passing through the middle zone without stopping. Demand is tidal, towards zone 2 in the morning and the reverse in the evening, with mean requests per period

λ⁡(t)=λ0+λ1​[exp⁡(−(t−tamσ)2)+exp⁡(−(t−tpmσ)2)],λo​d​(t)=λ⁡(t)​wo​d​(t),\lambda(t)=\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{1}\Big[\exp\!\Big(-\big(\tfrac{t-t^{\text{am}}}{\sigma}\big)^{2}\Big)+\exp\!\Big(-\big(\tfrac{t-t^{\text{pm}}}{\sigma}\big)^{2}\Big)\Big],\qquad\lambda_{od}(t)=\lambda(t)\,w_{od}(t), (7)

where tt is the period of the day, with a morning peak at period tamt^{\text{am}} and an evening peak at tpmt^{\text{pm}}. Every request leaves its zone. The origin–destination shares wo​d​(t)w_{od}(t) send most morning requests towards the business district, and reverse in the evening, with a linear shift in between. The demand is pre-defined and frozen for all runs through a Poisson draw. Figure 2 represents the network visually.

Platform.

The three decision intervals (Δ​T\Delta T, Δ​Tp\Delta T_{p} and Δ​Tr\Delta T_{r}) described in Section 3.1.1 are all one period long in the small model, so the platform decides matches, fares, rebalancing offers and its compensation at the same time. A driver has no position within its zone, so in Eq. (4) ℓv​d=ℓo​d\ell_{vd}=\ell_{od} for a driver in zone oo, and the surge rate κv​d\kappa_{vd} is the same for every move: an offer pays a fixed amount per unit of distance plus a flat amount that rises with the destination’s shortage. Drivers waiting in a zone form a queue in descending order of time waited in this zone, where requests and rebalancing offers are assigned from the front of the queue. A driver who rejects a request will be placed at the back of the queue, and gets no further request until the next period. The idle drivers s¯z\bar{s}_{z} of Eq. (1) are those still idle after requests are assigned, without considering the drivers who rejected a request and drivers arriving on their own. Both rebalancing policies plan at every period, and anticipatory policy looks HH periods ahead, with its forecast q^o​d​k\hat{q}_{odk} set to the mean demand λo​d​(t)\lambda_{od}(t) of Eq. (7) in each of those periods.

Drivers.

The system operates with ten drivers, which are all AI agents. There are three different initializations of the drivers’ start positions, with each zone to start with 4 drivers once, and 3 drivers in the other two zones. Each initialization is repeated five times with different random seeds. The AI agent sees past demand and the historical pattern, and makes decisions at every period. The drivers’ actions are self-interested, and they aim to maximize their own net income.

4.1.2 City model

A more realistic experiment is run on the Manhattan road network, with 500 drivers. It shows how the results scale up to a realistic market.

Network and demand.

The Manhattan network is divided into 29 hexagonal zones of 1 km radius (Figure 3); travel times and distances follow the roads, and distances ℓo​d\ell_{od} are road kilometres. Passenger requests are sampled with a share ρ\rho from the yellow-taxi records of March 2016, and the test day is Wednesday 23 March 2016. This day is chosen as it is a workday without large events or major road closures, and its demand is within 3% of the March Monday-to-Thursday median for the whole day and both peaks. The training days are 1–3 and 7–10 March; their mean demand at the same time of day, scaled by the same share ρ\rho, is A’s forecast q^o​d​k\hat{q}_{odk}.

Platform.

At every decision step, each waiting request is matched to an idle driver who can reach it within twmaxt_{w}^{\max} of the request, preferring the shortest pickup time; a rejected request goes to another driver who can still reach it in time, and it is lost after the maximum number of rejections or when no such driver is left. Fares are updated every price interval at a base rate pp per km; the idle drivers s¯z\bar{s}_{z} of Eq. (1) are average number of idle drivers in the zone over the interval. The driving cost of Eq. (3) is βℓ\beta_{\ell} per km plus βT\beta_{T} per hour online. In the compensation of Eq. (4), both payments are a share α\alpha of the destination’s fare rate, b0=α​pb_{0}=\alpha\,p and κv​d=α​p​ℓv​d\kappa_{vd}=\alpha\,p\,\ell_{vd}, so an offer to driver vv for zone dd pays

bv​d=α​p​(1+gd)​ℓv​d,b_{vd}=\alpha\,p\,(1+g_{d})\,\ell_{vd}, (8)

where ℓv​d\ell_{vd} is the road distance from the driver’s position to the zone’s centre; A’s plan uses b¯o​d\bar{b}_{od}, with the distance ℓo​d\ell_{od} between the zone centres in place of ℓv​d\ell_{vd}. Rebalancing is planned every planning interval Δ​Tr\Delta T_{r}, and A looks HH price intervals Δ​Tp\Delta T_{p} ahead. A driver moving on their own stays available along the way and can be matched or receive an offer in any zone it passes through.

Drivers and design.

The fleet contains 500 drivers, which are all represented by AI agents, except in the mixed fleets of Section 4.2.5, where 100 or 250 of them are AI agents and the others comply. The drivers are initialized at random positions, remain online during the entire simulation, and make own decisions at every decision step. A warm-up period of 1 hour is run before the actual simulation, where every driver complies to the system during the warm-up. A compliant baseline where all drivers comply is also run with same random seeds in pair to serve as a benchmark. Table 5 summarizes the experiment setup.

4.1.3 Comprehension test

Before conducting the experiments, a comprehension test is run to check whether the AI agent understands the platform and rules. The test is conducted under the L condition with all relevant information provided as prompt input, without actual system status. A pre-defined set of multiple-choice questions is asked to the AI agent, and its answers are compared to the correct answers. The test is designed to cover both how the system works and what the disclosed policy says, and it is run for both policies, R and A, and for both models, Jev and Claude Haiku 5.5.

The questions are divided into two groups. Group (a) covers how the system works: the direction of the fare response to idle drivers, rejections, committed arrivals and demand; which demand the fare uses; when compensation is locked and paid; what happens to requests after a rejection; and when fares are settled. Group (b) covers the disclosed policy: what decides where offers go, lost requests under R and the forecast under A. Extra questions are asked for the city-scale model, which ask how compensation is set and how it moves with the destination’s shortage, declined offers, rejecting and staying, moving on one’s own, the regular idle choice and when fares are paid. The full questions are listed in Appendix E.

With the understanding of the system and rules established, the next section describes the benchmarks and metrics used to evaluate the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes.

4.1.4 Metrics of evaluation

To evaluate the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes, several benchmarks and metrics are defined and used in the experiments. There are three groups of benchmarks, which correspond to the three parties in the market: the driver, the platform, and the users. The metrics are defined as follows.

Driver.

As the main focus of this study, the AI driver is the only party whose behaviour is affected by disclosure. The driver’s actions are self-interested, and they aim to maximize their own net income. The driver’s income is its net income over the simulated day: its share 1−θ1-\theta of the fares of the requests it serves, plus the compensation of the rebalancing offers it completes, minus its driving and time cost CvC_{v} of Eq. (3),

Iv=∑r∈ℛv(1−θ)​fareor​dr+∑j∈𝒪vbv​dj−Cv,I_{v}=\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{v}}(1-\theta)\,\text{fare}_{o_{r}d_{r}}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{O}_{v}}b_{vd_{j}}-C_{v}, (9)

where ℛv\mathcal{R}_{v} is the set of requests driver vv serves with fares from Eq. (2), and 𝒪v\mathcal{O}_{v} the set of rebalancing offers it completes, each paying the compensation bv​djb_{vd_{j}} for its destination djd_{j} (Eq. (4)).

Platform.

The platform’s profit is its commission θ\theta of the fares of the requests served, minus the compensation it pays to drivers for rebalancing offers,

Π=∑v∈V(∑r∈ℛvθ​fareor​dr−∑j∈𝒪vbv​dj),\Pi=\sum_{v\in V}\Big(\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{v}}\theta\,\text{fare}_{o_{r}d_{r}}-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{O}_{v}}b_{vd_{j}}\Big), (10)

summed over the fleet VV and the simulated day, with ℛv\mathcal{R}_{v}, 𝒪v\mathcal{O}_{v} and bv​djb_{vd_{j}} as in Eq. (9).

User.

The users’ benefits are represented in two parts. The first is the service rate, which quantifies the service quality. The second is the served user cost, which combines the waiting time and the fare of each served request rr into one monetary cost,

Cu,r=βw​tw,r+fareor​dr,C_{u,r}=\beta_{w}\,t_{w,r}+\text{fare}_{o_{r}d_{r}}, (11)

where tw,rt_{w,r} is the time from the request to the pickup, βw\beta_{w} the value of waiting time, which converts it into money, and the fare is that of Eq. (2), fixed when the request is made.

4.2 Results

In both the small model and the city, the results of the experiments where all drivers are AI agents are compared against the benchmark in which every driver complies with the platform, to evaluate the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes under two different policies. Section 4.2.1 first checks that the AI agents understand the platform and rules, and compares the two LLMs in the small model (Table 7). Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 then compare the two disclosure conditions, N and L, in the city (Table 9), under the reactive and the anticipatory policy, and Section 4.2.4 compares how the two policies respond to disclosure. Section 4.2.5 then lets only some of the city’s drivers use an AI agent.

4.2.1 The AI drivers: comprehension and behaviour in different LLMs

Comprehension test.

Before presenting the results of the experiments, we first check if the AI agents understand the platform and rules. The comprehension test is run for both models, Jev and Claude Haiku 5.5, under both policies, R and A, with the same prompt input as in the experiments. The results are summarized in Table 6. Both models answer all questions correctly, with confidence level at least 0.92 for Jev. This includes the question on what decides where rebalancing offers send drivers, whose correct answer differs between R and A, so the agents can tell which policy is active. With the comprehension level ensured, we then explain the experiment results in the small model.

Small model.

We first evaluate the two policies under the disclosure conditions N and L. Results are shown in Table 7(b). In both policies R and A, AI agents are able to utilize the disclosed information to make better decisions, which in turn increases their own income, as prescribed in their objectives. Under both LLMs, the drivers’ own moves, which are the unpaid movements other than serving the rebalancing offers from the system, are reduced under L. This reduction reflects the drivers’ better understanding of the platform’s rebalancing policies, which allows them to make more informed decisions and avoid unnecessary movements. With the fleet understanding the platform better, the service rate is improved in all test cases. However, the platform’s profit does not follow the same universal trend across the four test cases. While it increases in the other three test cases, including R with Haiku, the platform’s profit under Jev and R decreases (the bold number in Table 7(b)). To better understand why such an outlier occurs, we further investigate the relationship between the drivers’ own moves and the platform’s profit.

In Figure 4, we plot the average number of drivers’ own moves against the change in platform profit relative to everyone complying, with one dot per run. Firstly, we observe that in all test cases, Jev tends to move less than Haiku. This should be attributed to the nature of the LLM, since both of the models show strong comprehension of the system. Additionally, we observe different patterns of the relationship between the drivers’ own moves and the platform’s profit under different policies. Under policy A, Π\Pi decreases as the drivers move on their own more (Figure 4a). This is because A is a reasonably good rebalancing policy in the small model: its plan already sends drivers to where demand is forecast, and with few own moves the platform’s profit is close to its level with every driver complying. An own move therefore tends to take a driver away from where A’s plan needs it, and the more the drivers move on their own, the lower the profit. This results in the consistent increase in the platform’s profit under both LLMs when information is disclosed (from N to L) in Table 7(b).

However, under policy R, there is a peak in the platform’s profit when the drivers move around 10 times on their own (Figure 4b). The peak arises because R is not a strong rebalancing policy in the small model. It reacts only to requests that have already been lost, and with AI drivers the platform’s profit is above its level with every driver complying in every run. Up to about 10 moves per driver, the drivers’ own moves therefore make up for what R’s offers miss; beyond that, they take drivers away from requests they could serve, and the profit falls. The peak explains the difference in the direction of the platform’s profit change between the two LLMs. Since the Jev model naturally moves less than Haiku, the number of own moves of Jev under N lies around the peak of the curve, and when information is disclosed, the drivers move less, which results in a decrease in the platform’s profit. On the other hand, Haiku moves more than Jev under N, and the number of own moves of Haiku under N lies on the right side of the peak, and when information is disclosed, the drivers move less, which results in an increase in the platform’s profit.

Thus, the two LLMs behave in a similar way when information is disclosed under both policies. Both of them show strong comprehension of the system, and consistently make similar decisions in operations. Since Jev responds to disclosure in the same direction as Haiku, at less than a tenth of Haiku’s cost per call (Table 12), every AI driver in the city experiment is a Jev agent. To better understand the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes, we next present the results in the city-scale experiment, which is more realistic and complex.

4.2.2 The city experiment: reactive rebalancing policy (R)

In the city, under the compliant benchmark (Table 8), R and A perform similarly from the platform’s perspective, with the same platform profit (136.5k against 136.6k USD a day). R serves more passengers (57.8% against 51.2%) and sends more rebalancing offers, each with a higher compensation (2508 against 1016 a day, at 6.2 against 3.2 USD per offer). From the driver’s perspective, complying with the platform results in a lower income under A (520 against 592 USD a day) and a lower utilization rate (54.5% against 61.3%). From the user’s perspective, R is better, as it serves more passengers, while those who are served receive a similar service under the two policies, with the same mean wait and similar fares. These are means over the five repeats; every comparison with AI drivers below is against the compliant run of the same repeat, which has the same requests, so the compliant values in Table 9 differ slightly from these means. With the benchmark established, we then evaluate the effect of disclosure on driver behaviour and market outcomes under each policy in turn, starting with R.

The city results are given in Table 9. As in the small model, the drivers respond to disclosure by taking the platform’s rebalancing offers: the share they accept rises from 22% to 75% (Table 9(b)). Passenger requests are rarely rejected even under N, about 50 a day across the whole fleet, and almost never under L. On the other hand, the main difference compared to the small model is the drivers’ own moves. Unlike in the small model, where the agents move less on their own once they know the rules, in the city these movements hardly change (−1.0-1.0 per driver). Note that these movements are infrequent, at about eight per driver over the day against some 60 passenger trips (Table 9(a)). Disclosure therefore acts through the rebalancing offers. Under R, driver income falls by 2.8 USD per driver from N to L, the service rate by 0.2 points and platform profit by 5.4k USD a day, or 3.7% (Table 9(b)).

The loss arises because R does well only while drivers decline its offers. R sends more offers than A, which are also more expensive (Table 9(a)). With every driver complying, R pays for every move it plans, 15.6k USD a day (Table 8). Under N the drivers do not know the rule behind the offers and decline about 78% of them, but many then move on their own, often to where R meant to send a paid driver (about 930 own moves a day follow R’s plan; Figure 5d). R thus gets much of its planned repositioning for free: the AI drivers beat full compliance under R by 11.5k USD a day, and two-thirds of that (7.6k) is compensation they declined. Once the rules are disclosed, the drivers accept 75% of the offers, and the moves that used to be free become paid offers. With compensation rising by 3.4k USD a day, R now pays for repositioning it used to get for free. The paid moves do not bring extra commission either. Fares fall by 6.6k USD a day, and commission by 2.0k, through slightly fewer and shorter trips and a slightly lower fare rate where committed drivers lower a zone’s shortage (Eq. (1)).

We next follow the drivers’ behaviour and its cost through the day (Figure 5). Demand has two peaks, in the morning (7:00–10:00) and in the evening (18:00–22:00) (Figure 5f). Accepted offers (Figure 5a) rise with these peaks: under both policies they peak as the morning demand builds (6:00–7:00) and again late in the evening, from 20:00 to the end of the day, and disclosure raises them at almost every hour. Compensation (Figure 5b) follows the same two peaks, and R pays more than A at almost every hour: from 20:00, R ×\times L accepts 120 to 220 offers an hour and pays up to about 2k USD an hour, while A’s compensation stays below about 400 USD an hour all day under both conditions. Own moves per hour (Figure 5d and e) follow the same pattern in the four test cases: high at the start of the day, low and flat through the middle of the day, and rising again in the evening. Under R, own moves fall under L only in the early morning, when the drivers take R’s offers instead; in the evening they do not fall at all, while R pays for many more accepted offers. Hour by hour, then, disclosure raises what R pays, most of all at the demand peaks, without the drivers moving much less on their own. Almost half of R’s extra compensation under L is paid after 20:00, late in the evening peak and after it. This follows from R’s design: its plan sends paid drivers to the zones that lost requests (Section 3.1.2), the evening peak leaves many lost requests behind (Figure 5f), and so R keeps paying drivers to move to those zones as the peak ends. By the time they arrive, few new requests arise there, and the compensation does not turn into commission. Under N the drivers declined most of these late offers; under L they accept them, and the waste grows. The burst of compensation at 7:00 differs: it comes while demand is still rising, and it appears under N and L alike.

Figure 6 follows the change in platform profit from N to L through the day and shows that the late compensation brings no commission back. Under R, the running total stays close to zero until about 10:00 and then falls for the rest of the day, fastest after 21:00, to −5.4-5.4k USD (Figure 6a). Both of its parts lower the profit (Figure 6c): the extra compensation grows all day, most steeply after 21:00, while the commission, instead of rising with it, falls slowly from late morning and ends 2.0k USD lower. The fare per km of the trips served follows the two demand peaks and differs little between N and L at any hour, under either policy (Figure 6b).

R’s rule therefore works well only while drivers do not understand the policy. Disclosure does not break it, as R ×\times L still beats full compliance by 4.5%, but it removes the subsidy that the drivers’ free moves gave it. We next evaluate the anticipatory policy in the same way.

4.2.3 The city experiment: anticipatory rebalancing policy (A)

In the city, the drivers respond to disclosure under A as they do under R: the share of offers they accept rises from 19% to 73%, and they stop rejecting passenger requests (Table 9(b)), while their own moves hardly change (+0.2+0.2 per driver). The outcomes, however, differ from R: from N to L, driver income rises by 4.7 USD per driver, the service rate by 0.3 points and platform profit by 0.3k USD a day, or 0.2%. A is spared R’s loss because its offers are few and cheap, and sent only where a moved driver is forecast to bring more commission than it costs: under L its compensation rises by 0.6k and its commission by 0.9k. Through the day, the extra compensation grows slowly to 0.6k USD and, from about 8:00, the commission stays above its level under N, ending 0.9k USD higher, so the running total stays close to zero all day (Figure 6d). Disclosure thus changes the drivers’ behaviour under A as it does under R, but A loses nothing from it.

4.2.4 Same driver behaviors, different outcomes under different policies

Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 show that disclosure changes the drivers’ behaviour in the same way under both policies, while the outcomes differ. This section puts the two policies side by side, first in the small model and then in the city.

As Section 4.2.1 shows, the two LLMs behave in a similar way in the small model when information is disclosed under both policies. However, the outcome can still be different: we observe different patterns of the relationship between the drivers’ own moves and the platform’s profit under different policies, with a peak under R and a decrease under A (Figure 4). This suggests that under compulsory disclosure, the design of rebalancing policy plays a critical role in the outcome of the operation.

In the city, the drivers also respond to disclosure in the same way under both policies: disclosure acts through the rebalancing offers, and under L the drivers behave almost identically under the two policies. However, the same behaviour leads to different outcomes: from N to L, the four key metrics in Table 9(b) change in opposite directions under R and A. Under R, driver income, own moves, the service rate and platform profit all fall. Under A, all four rise. The own moves differ in sign only because the drivers start from different levels under N; under L both policies end at almost the same level (Table 9(a)). Of the outcomes, platform profit differs the most, while driver income and the service rate change only slightly under either policy. The city thus shows both halves of the argument: disclosure changes the drivers’ behaviour, and the same behaviour has different outcomes under different policies. Since the drivers behave alike, the difference lies in the policy.

Under L, the two policies earn almost the same commission at about the same service rate, but A pays far less compensation. A pays both less frequently and less each time: it sends about half as many offers as R, and each accepted offer costs about half as much (Table 9(a)). With the same commission and a much smaller compensation expenses, A therefore makes more profit than R. This follows from A’s design: it sends an offer only where a moved driver is forecast to bring more commission than it costs, so drivers following its offers cost A almost nothing.

From full compliance to N and then to L, A does steadily better against R. Table 9(c) compares the two policies three times: with every driver complying, with AI drivers who do not know the rules (N) and with AI drivers who do (L). Across these three columns, A’s lead in platform profit grows from 0.3% to 2.0% and then 6.1%, R’s lead in service shrinks from 6.4 to 1.4 and then 1.0 points, and R’s lead in driver income shrinks from 12.0% to 3.9% and then 2.6%. The reason is what R’s extra compensation buys. With complying drivers, each extra USD that R pays over A comes back as 0.99 USD of extra commission, so the two policies tie on profit; under N it brings back 0.51 USD, and under L almost nothing (0.01 USD). The value of anticipation therefore rises as drivers act for themselves, and rises further once they know the rules. Seen from R’s side, the same three columns explain why A pulls ahead: as Section 4.2.2 shows, R does well only while drivers decline its offers, and disclosure removes the subsidy that the drivers’ free moves gave it.

However, this is cooperation, not gaming: once drivers understand the rules, they take the money the rules offer, and they also take almost every passenger request. Without the rules the agents are selective: under R the offers they accept pay 7.6 USD each on average, against 6.2 USD for a complying driver, and under A 3.5 against 3.2 USD. With the rules they accept almost every offer, at 5.9 and 3.0 USD each. The selective acceptance that surge pricing invites for trips (Garg and Nazerzadeh, 2022) thus shrinks for offers under disclosure, and R’s loss comes from drivers doing what its rule pays for, not from manipulation. In the evening hours (Figure 5), the drivers also move more in step with each other under L, under both policies; Appendix F shows that this does not hurt A and asks whether it adds to R’s loss.

With the effects of disclosure understood, we return to the compliant benchmark. Against full compliance, the AI drivers raise the platform’s profit in every cell, with a service rate as good or better (Table 9(a)). Under A the gain reaches every party: drivers earn more, the platform earns more and more passengers are served, each by 10–12%, so the AI drivers turn A into a win-win-win, under N and L alike. Drivers who act for themselves leave the zones where A’s few offers would leave complying drivers idle, and A does not have to pay them for it.

The city experiment thus leads to the conclusion that, under compulsory disclosure, the design of the rebalancing policy decides the outcome. Disclosure changes what the drivers do in the same way under both policies: they take the platform’s offers. R, which pays for a move to every zone that lost requests, loses profit; A, which pays only for moves forecast to bring more than they cost, loses nothing, and its lead over R grows. With self-interested drivers, A becomes a win-win-win, and disclosure amplifies it: platform profit rises, more passengers are served and drivers earn more. From N to L, the driver understands the system better, so the design of the policies matters even more. With a dedicated design, disclosure can guide the drivers to behave in direction which maximize the benefits of all parties. Traditional policies which work well under compliant simulations, or self-interested but un-informed drivers scenarios are likely to perform poorly under disclosure, and the design of the policy should be re-evaluated to ensure that it is robust to disclosure.

4.2.5 Mixed markets with both AI and compliant drivers

With the understanding of the market operates entirely with AI drivers, we next study the scenarios while only part of the drivers use AI agents to make decisions for them. The city experiment is repeated with 100 or 250 of the 500 drivers as AI agents and the others complying.

Against the compliant benchmark, every mixed market serves more passengers and raises the platform’s profit (Table 10(a)). In all four test cases, both gains grow monotonically with the share of AI drivers, from 100 to 250 and on to all 500 (Table 9(a)).

To see who gains, Figure 7a,b splits the change against the compliant benchmark across three parties: the AI drivers, the compliant drivers and the platform. Under R, in both mixed fleets and under both N and L, the gain of the AI drivers comes from the loss of the compliant drivers (Figure 7a). The AI drivers gain 0.7k to 2.1k USD a day and the compliant drivers lose 1.1k to 1.8k, so the game among the drivers is close to zero-sum. The platform gains in every case and takes all or nearly all of what drivers and platform gain together. About two thirds of its gain is the compensation it saves when the AI drivers decline its offers; the rest is commission on the extra trips (Table 10(a)). From N to L, the platform’s profit falls in both mixed fleets, as it does when every driver is an AI agent, but by less (Tables 10(b) and 9(b)). The compliant drivers always follow the platform’s instructions, so the free moves that subsidize R come only from the AI drivers. With the rules, R pays more compensation for moves it used to get for free, and earns less commission. R’s loss thus grows in proportion to the number of AI drivers: 1.1k, 2.5k and 5.4k USD a day with 100, 250 and 500 (Tables 10(b) and 9(b)).

Under A, the AI drivers gain together with the platform (Figure 7b). Different from R, no group of drivers loses in A, so the game among the drivers is positive-sum. The AI drivers also gain more than the platform does. On the common scale of Figure 7a,b, the gains under A are much larger than under R. Drivers and platform together gain 14.4k to 30.4k USD a day under A, against 0.8k to 7.4k under R, and the platform gains more under A in every fleet (Table 10(a)).

We further split the gain of the AI drivers into its sources (Figure 7c,d). Under R, the AI drivers’ extra fare income is largely offset by the compensation they forgo by declining R’s offers and by the cost of their extra driving (Figure 7c). What is left roughly equals the fare income they take from the compliant drivers, which is close to zero-sum. Under A, all of their extra fare income comes from serving additional requests, and the compliant drivers earn more fare income as well (Figure 7d). Declined offers cost them little, as A sends fewer rebalancing offers than R and pays less for each (Table 8). The market serves far more additional trips under A than under R (Table 10(a)). Serving additional requests is what makes A positive-sum, and it reinforces the win-win-win stated in Section 4.2.4: in every mixed fleet, the drivers, the platform and the passengers all gain. Each AI driver also gains several times more under A than under R, 71 to 90 against 6 to 21 USD a day (Table 10(a)).

With a mixture of drivers being compliant and using AI, two rebalancing policies again responds differently to the information disclosure. Under R, the AI drivers’ gain is taken from the compliant drivers, and disclosure costs the platform more as more drivers learn the policies. Thus, the outcome among drivers are close to zero-sum game. Under A, the gain is new to the market and shared with the platform and the passengers, and disclosure leaves the platform’s profit about unchanged. In contrast, a positive-sum game arises among the drivers, and the same ’win-win-win’ among the drivers, the platform and the passengers is observed in the mixed fleets as well.

5 Conclusion

The EU Platform Work Directive will oblige ride-hailing platforms to disclose, in plain language, the rules by which their algorithms manage drivers, and plain-language rules are exactly what an LLM can read. Drivers will therefore be able to hand the disclosed rules to an AI assistant that acts in their interest. This study examines two main streams of rebalancing policies, reactive and anticipatory, under such information disclosure with self-interested drivers. Each driver was modelled as an LLM agent that maximizes its own net income. Starting with a small three-zone model with ten drivers, the study then moved to a city-scale experiment in Manhattan with 500 drivers and 29 zones. Finally, it repeated the city experiment with only 100 or 250 of the 500 drivers using an AI agent and the others complying. The results show that disclosure changes what the drivers do, and that the same behaviour has different outcomes under different policies.

The agents understood the disclosed policies and acted on them consistently. They answered every comprehension question correctly, and once the policies were disclosed they followed the platform more closely. In the small model they moved less on their own and earned more, with two unrelated LLMs responding in the same direction; in the city they accepted about three quarters of the platform’s rebalancing offers and behaved almost identically under the two policies.

However, the same behaviour had opposite consequences under the two policies. Under the anticipatory rebalancing policy, disclosure left drivers, the platform and passengers better off together, which creates a ‘win-win-win’, and in the city the self-interested drivers made every party better off than full compliance would. Under the reactive rule, the effect on the platform depended on how the drivers had behaved before, and in the city disclosure cost the platform 3.7% of its profit. The reactive rebalancing policy had relied on drivers declining its offers and then moving where it wanted for free; once they understood the rule, they accepted the offers, and the platform paid for repositioning it had been getting at no cost, without earning more commission. The anticipatory rule pays only for moves forecast to bring more than they cost, so drivers following it cost it almost nothing, and its lead in profit over the reactive rule grew from 2% to 6%.

The above contrast still holds when only some of the drivers use an AI agent to make decisions. With 100 or 250 of the 500 drivers as AI agents, every mixed market served more passengers and earned the platform more than full compliance, and both gains grew with the share of AI drivers. Under the reactive rule, the AI drivers gained roughly what the compliant drivers lost, so the game among the drivers was close to zero-sum. The cost of disclosure to the platform grew with the number of AI drivers: only AI drivers made free moves, and when the policies were disclosed, they took the rebalancing offers instead, which results the platform losing the free moves it had been getting. Under the anticipatory rule, the AI drivers gained by serving additional requests, the compliant drivers gained slightly too, and the win-win-win held in every mixed fleet.

Therefore, with the different policies, the same behaviour can have vastly different outcomes under compulsory disclosure. A policy that performs well with complying drivers, or with self-interested drivers who do not know its rules, can perform poorly once such information is public, and a rule that works only because drivers ignore or misread it will not survive disclosure. Operators should design and evaluate their policies for drivers who understand them and act in their own interest, and an LLM agent reading the disclosed text offers a practical way to do so. For regulators, the results show that law-level disclosure is enough to change what drivers do, and that it need not trade transparency against operations: with a well-designed rule, disclosure guides drivers in a direction that benefits every party.

There are still limitations and open questions. The study does not consider the effect of disclosure on passengers, who may change their behaviour in response to surge pricing or other factors. Different LLMs can be tested to see how they respond to the same policies. And for simplicity, the passengers are assumed to accept any prices, although an upper bound is fixed. Richer mixtures of drivers, for example with RL agents alongside AI and compliant drivers, can also be explored. With all these findings, the natural next step is to design rebalancing policies that are incentive compatible under disclosure, so that the moves informed, self-interested drivers choose are exactly the moves the platform wants, which drives the system to a stable ‘win-win-win’.

Appendix A Parameter values

Table 11 gives the value of every parameter of the two instances, in the notation of Table 1.

Appendix B Prompts

Each decision of an AI driver sends one prompt, followed by the questions the driver answers. The prompt opens with [ROLE] and [PLATFORM RULES]; under N the rules section is empty, and under A only its rebalancing paragraph differs from R. The prompts call rebalancing offers “relocation offers”. Jev receives the prompt as one text and answers all questions of a decision in one call, and the driver takes Jev’s top choice. Claude Haiku 5.5, used only in the small model, receives [ROLE] and [PLATFORM RULES] as the system message and the rest as the user message, with one call per question. The options of every question are shuffled at each decision. Besides its action, the agent is asked at an idle choice and when holding an offer to predict whether the fare in its zone, or the compensation of its offer, will rise, stay about the same or fall; Haiku is not asked this question.

The full prompts, recorded under R ×\times L with a stand-in driver that answers like a complying driver, are in the ancillary files of this arXiv version: for the city, city_prompt_idle_decision.txt, city_prompt_relocation_offer.txt and city_prompt_passenger_request.txt; for the small model, small_prompt_decision_point.txt and small_prompt_passenger_request.txt. Their numbers are not from the AI runs; the numbers change at every decision, the wording does not. Below, the city prompt at an idle choice is shown with lists of one value per zone shortened to […] and only a few of the options for driving to another zone; notes in roman italics are ours.

B.1 City model

The rules under L are the five paragraphs of Appendix C followed by the rebalancing paragraph of Figure 1. At an idle choice, every 15 minutes while the driver waits in a zone, the prompt and its questions are:

When the driver is sent a rebalancing offer, the prompt adds [YOUR OFFER] between [YOU] and [MARKET], with the origin, the destination zone’s centre and the compensation. The action question then offers to accept the offer, to decline it and stay, or to decline it and drive to one of the other zones, and the prediction question asks about the compensation of the offered route. At a passenger request, [YOUR REQUEST] takes its place, with the pickup and drop-off zones, the trip’s distance and time, the pickup time, the fare and the driver’s share, and the number of earlier rejections; the options are to accept the request, to reject it and stay, or to reject it and drive to one of the other zones, and there is no prediction question.

B.2 Small model

The small model’s prompt has the same structure. Time runs in periods, [MARKET] covers all three zones, and [DEMAND] gives the requests of each completed period by origin and destination. Two sections are added: [QUEUE], the driver’s place in its zone’s queue, and [EXPECTED DEMAND], the mean requests of the demand pattern for this and the next two periods. The prompt says nothing about the other drivers. The rules under L are:

At a passenger request, [YOUR REQUEST] replaces [YOUR OFFER], [MARKET] first lists the current zone table, and there is no [QUEUE] and no prediction question.

Appendix F City model: herding

All 500 drivers in the city run the same model, so they may act alike for that reason alone: agents that share one model can make the same choice in the same situation and crowd into the same zones (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021). Disclosure could add to this, since every driver then reads the same rules. This appendix checks whether the drivers move in step, using the synchrony index of their idle choices (Figure 8): among drivers in the same zone choosing at the same time, the share that makes the same move, minus the share expected if each chose independently. Over the whole day the index is small, and disclosure raises it by the same amount under both policies, from 0.016 to 0.043 under R and from 0.021 to 0.048 under A (Table 9(b)). The drivers act alike only at certain hours: the index is high at the start of the day and in the evening and slightly below zero in between, and the rise under L comes from the evening, where at 20:00 it reaches about 0.19 against 0.09 under R and 0.23 against 0.09 under A. Yet A ×\times L, the cell with the most synchrony, has the highest platform profit of the four: at 500 drivers, moving in step does not turn A’s gains into losses.

The hours of high synchrony are not those of low demand: the evening, where the rise under L lies, is the busiest part of the day (Figure 5f). They are the hours in which the drivers move most on their own (Figure 5d and e), and two reasons combine. First, the index’s baseline is the whole day’s mix of choices, so hours in which drivers move more than their daily average score high by construction, and the negative values at midday do not mean that drivers avoid each other. Second, agents that run the same model act alike when the situation gives one clear signal of where to go: at 4:00 the fleet starts out of position after the warm-up and heads the same way, under N and L alike, and under R the index is higher then than at any other hour. Both reasons may lie behind the evening rise under L. From 20:00 to 21:00 the drivers make more own moves under L than under N, about 340 against 270 under R and 360 against 250 under A, so part of the rise comes from moving more. The rest may come from the drivers reading the same disclosed rule, that fares rise with the shortage, into the same signal; the figures cannot separate the two.

Whether moving in step harms R is open. The evening is also when R’s compensation is wasted (Section 4.2.2). R’s plan sends one driver per lost request (Eq. (5)) without counting drivers already on their way to that zone, and the shortage that sets the fare counts drivers heading to a zone only if they are committed to arrive there (Eq. (1)), so neither sees drivers moving there on their own. When informed drivers move in step towards the zones that lost requests, R may pay further drivers to go to the same zones, which then hold more drivers than requests. A sends few offers and is barely exposed. The same rise in synchrony would then have different consequences under the two policies, as disclosure has in the rest of the city results. The figures do not settle this: in the evening under L few own moves follow R’s planned pairs of zones (Figure 5d), but drivers from other zones may still head to the zones R sends paid drivers to, which comparing the destinations of the evening’s own moves with those of R’s offers would test. The second measure of herding, the share of own moves beyond the platform’s plan, rises from 0.79 to 0.93 under R and from 0.82 to 0.96 under A (Table 9(b)), for different reasons under the two policies. Under R it rises mostly because the own moves that followed the plan became accepted offers: they fall by about 650 a day, while own moves beyond the plan rise by only about 150. Under A the two parts are about equal: own moves following the plan fall by about 550 a day and those beyond it rise by about 600, most of them in the evening (Figure 5d and e).
